source.title: Reliability Scaling Laws for Quantized Large Language Models
source.authors: Sirine Ayadi; S'andor Dar'oczi; Stephan Günnemann; Bertrand Charpentier

record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling-trend analysis to quantized models and total model bits, and reports downstream-task performance trends; it does not test the original pretraining-loss or compute-allocation laws.
record.gate_note: The study measures performance and reliability while varying quantization, model size, and total model bits. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, training tokens, or training compute, or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Reliability outcomes are related scaling results but are not among the listed claim versions; they are recorded with versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The study reports downstream accuracy as model size and total model bits vary across LLaMA-3, OPT and Qwen3 base and post-training-quantized models, with log-quadratic fits in log(bits). This bears on V6 in a new setting, inference-time quantization. It does not measure pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute, fit power laws, or study allocation or shape (V1–V5, V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude accuracy scales monotonically with total model bits, while reliability scales nonlinearly and peaks for moderately sized 4-bit models. Quantization, not pruning, can improve robustness to natural perturbations. They stress that they fit empirical log-quadratic trends and do not propose a formal predictive law.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies post-training quantization and total model bits, then evaluates downstream performance and reliability. It does not fit pretraining loss against parameter count, token count, or training compute, nor estimate a compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports ablations across sampling temperatures 0.2, 0.7, and 1.0 and different output lengths; overall trends are described as consistent, but at higher temperatures 3-bit models yield the best Brier scores at fixed total bits. Perturbation intensity (4 or 16) is also varied.

fits_no_version.finding: Reliability metrics (AUCROC entropy, calibration) scale non-monotonically with total bits. Larger 4/8/16-bit models show lower AUCROC, while 2-bit reliability improves with scale.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Uncertainty/calibration reliability of LLMs does not improve monotonically with scale or total model bits.

fits_no_version.finding: KL divergence of quantized models from their full-precision bases depends on bitwidth and shrinks with size for 3-bit.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Quantization-induced distribution shift decreases with model size at low precision.

record.problems: Many scaling trends are reported qualitatively or in figures without numerical values in the text. Evaluations use 1000 sampled prompts for most datasets, generated sequences are limited to 20 tokens in the main setup, and some ablations use 100 TriviaQA samples.
record.rows_left_out: No other claim-relevant results were omitted. Reliability and KL-divergence outcomes were included as versions ["none"]; other compression and reliability findings not tied to the listed versions are summarized in gate_note or authors_conclusion.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a power law in parameters, tokens or compute. Perplexity is shown only against total model bits for off-the-shelf models, with no power-law fit.
Extrapolation from small fitted runs to much larger runs.
Depth/width/shape effects at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer regimes.
Predictability of downstream performance from pretraining loss. A priori prediction or extrapolation of downstream scores; the authors say they propose no predictive law.
Dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal split on fitting choices.

missing.what: Base-model TriviaQA accuracy by size: 0.338 (1B), 0.549 (3B), 0.691 (8B), 0.728 (70B), plus values at perturbation intensities 4/16. These are the only numeric downstream-scaling values.
Perplexity on WikiText-2/PTB/C4 improving steadily with total model bits for base and quantized models.
missing.versions: none (adjacent to V1, but no power-law fit and models not controlled for tokens/compute)

missing.what: Downstream accuracy scaling with bits on MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC, CoQA, RACE, PiQA for LLaMA and Qwen3, and for instruction-tuned LLaMA.
Pruned models: performance degrades with sparsity, but performance of 50%/2:4-sparse models improves significantly with model scale.

record.verdict_notes: Scale here is total model bits (parameters × precision) of off-the-shelf models with differing training data, not controlled pretraining runs. Evidence is mostly qualitative and read from figures. Evaluations use 1000 sampled prompts per dataset and 20-token generations. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only as background.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameter count, training tokens, or training compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small training runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation, and how either scales with training compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities and training regimes such as repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study tests downstream performance trends against total model bits in quantized models, not predictability from pretraining loss or from parameter count alone.
Dependence of the original loss-law exponents or compute-optimal split on fitting choices, and departures of pretraining-loss curves from a power law.

rows.subject: LLaMA-3.2-1B, LLaMA-3.2-3B, LLaMA-3-8B, and LLaMA-3-70B base and quantized models

rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream accuracy across quantized model configurations as total model bits varied.

conditions.value: base and quantized configurations, including 2-, 3-, 4-, 8-, and 16-bit settings where available

rows.value: The text reports that performance improves with increased total model bits; 4-bit quantization improves accuracy relative to 16-bit at a fixed total-bit budget, while the trend reverses when precision is reduced further to 3 or 2 bits.
rows.note: The text gives qualitative trends across the evaluated configurations; it does not provide numerical accuracy values in the passage.
rows.check: Link is fine. The value mixes two findings: monotone improvement with bits, which bears on V6, and dependence on precision at a fixed bit budget. The fitted law is log-quadratic in log(bits), not a power law. 'Scale' also confounds LLaMA-3.2 and LLaMA-3 models with different training data.

rows.subject: OPT models
rows.operation_detail: Extended bit-level performance and reliability analysis to OPT models.
rows.value: The authors report that the scaling behavior aligns with their earlier findings and that 4-bit quantization generally offers the best trade-off between accuracy, reliability, and efficiency.
rows.note: Qualitative cross-architecture result; no numerical values are supplied in the passage.
rows.check: The text says 'six base models' but lists five sizes (350M–30B). The evidence is purely qualitative, from Figure 7a.

rows.subject: Qwen3 models
rows.operation_detail: Extended bit-level performance analysis to Qwen3 models and additional benchmarks.

conditions.value: CEval and additional benchmarks described in Sections 5.2 and D

rows.value: The authors report a generally favorable 4-bit trade-off; for Qwen models, 3-bit quantization of moderate-to-large models can also yield favorable zero-shot performance.
rows.note: The reported pattern is not uniform across precisions; the passage gives qualitative findings.
rows.check: State should be observed, not partial. The text says scaling 'aligns with our earlier findings'. The favorable 3-bit result for Qwen concerns which precision is best, not whether accuracy improves with scale.

source_check.notes: The fitted curves describe observed trends, not validated predictive extrapolation. Section 5.2 says six OPT base models but lists only five sizes.

statements.correction: Qwen3 sizes: 4B, 8B, 14B, 32B. Section 5.2: downstream performance improves with total model bits; reducing precision from 16 to 4 bits at fixed total bits improves accuracy; further reduction to 3 or 2 bits reverses that advantage in the main LLaMA analysis. Moderate-to-large Qwen3 models can perform favorably at 3 bits. Section 4: empirical log-quadratic fits; no formal predictive law or reported held-out extrapolation test.
statements.problem: The study contains no Qwen3-below-2B collapse experiment, adjusted R² results, reasoning plateau at N≥4B, or held-out memorization MAEs of 0.0946 and 0.0219. Calibration-set dependence and failed 2-bit fits are also unsupported. The fixed-bit precision trade-off is supported.
